claims.assertion: The trip is RydeTAXI (metered), and the record shows 21.7 km driven against a 16.3 km optimal route (+5.4 km, +33%), so excess mileage entered the metered fare and is refundable under RD-2.
The GPS track contains exactly two off-route segments: 17:04–17:11 adding 2.44 km (F3) and 17:18–17:23 adding 2.58 km (F4); each is reviewed separately under RD-1/RD-3/RD-4/RD-5.

For the first segment, the driver asked at 17:01 whether he could go round via Bedok North Road (F9) and the rider replied at 17:02 “Sure, your call.” (F10), before that segment started at 17:04 (F3); but this trip is not an expressway trip — the named road is Bedok North Road while the jam discussed was on the PIE (F9, F13) — and no fact places the 17:04–17:11 segment on Bedok North Road, so the tie is unproven and the segment is undetermined under G13 rather than a covered named route.

The rider’s message F10 is at most a general route choice (“your call”) over the pre-departure jam near the start; it cannot reach a second, later diversion that the rider never agreed to, as the complaint states and the driver himself concedes in F12.

For the second segment 17:18–17:23 (+2.58 km, F4) there is no rider message before it: the only rider message is F10 at 17:02, and the driver’s written statement F12 concedes “the second turn-off was my GPS rerouting”, so the segment was taken without a mutual agreement and is unexempted.

The driver’s post-trip assertion in F12 that “the rider agreed” cannot supply consent because consent must be a rider message sent before the segment (F10 is the rider’s only message, at 17:02), and an unrecorded/after-the-fact claim does not count.

The record contradicts the driver’s jam defence for the second segment: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F15), and the only congestion shown is speed band 4 on the PIE and CTE at 30–39 km/h (F13, F14), which is neither a band 1/2 condition nor a DataMall incident on the replaced optimal route, so RD-4 gives no exemption.
Because the second segment is not exempt, its extra 2.58 km must be refunded at this trip’s per-km rate of $1.4100/km (F5, F8), i.e. 2.58 × $1.4100 = $3.64, rounded to the nearest cent.

The refundable mileage is only the unexempted segment; the fare’s billed excess of 5.36 km (F5) includes route-corridor and matching mileage not attributed to any segment, which RD-2 leaves out of the refund.
The driver has 3 disputes with 2 upheld in the last 90 days, both route matters (F18), so this case makes his route deviation “repeated” and a flag_account referral is warranted alongside the refund.

No safety escalation is triggered on this record: the chat is two timestamped messages (F9–F11), the complaint and driver statement contain no threat, harassment or dangerous-driving allegation, so the case stays in the fare/deviations track.

weaknesses: The rider’s own “Sure, your call.” (F10) can be read as a broad general route authorisation covering the first segment, and if the first segment (F3) is exempted the refundable amount drops to only the second segment’s $3.64 — the driver will argue exactly this on the strength of F9+F10.

For the first segment (F3) the ground is undetermined rather than clearly unlawful: F9 names Bedok North Road and a stop or route record tying that segment to that road would flip it to named_road_tied under RD-5/G13 — the judge may find the rider agreed to it.

The driver will use the ongoing PIE congestion (F13, band 4, i.e. 30–39 km/h, not severe) to argue RD-4 reasonable cause for routing away from the expressway, and if the judge accepts it as covering the whole diversion no refund is due.
No fact puts the 17:18–17:23 segment on any route requested by anyone, so the driver can argue it was merely GPS re-optimisation within a consented route corridor rather than an unexempted deviation.
